# The coordinator's knowledge base

Boot, at session start and after every compaction, in this order: `CLAUDE.md`
→ `explorations/protocol.md` → `FACTS.md` (whole, in one pass) →
`POSITIONS.md` → `INDEX.md`, then `check-index.sh` run and every note it
reports missing given its line (Pavol, 2026-09-24) →
`explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`, first section → the boot note
(`postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md`, line 7). If the boot note says a batch
is running, its `CLIMB-BATCH-*.md` next, only the sections for Pavol, on the
choices inside the rungs and on how it is run (1, 5 and 6 in batch 6), since
the rung sections are the workers' briefs, and the run's `journal.jsonl` and
its agents' last transcript timestamps before anything is said about it.
Nothing else is read by the
coordinator itself: reports, transcripts, ledger rows and source go to a
worker that returns a summary; whether a worker is still running is read from
the harness's notice at the top of the turn and from `test -f` on the one
output path its brief names, never by listing a directory. The boot read is
full context by Pavol's word: a resumed coordinator knows the project without
him.

The coordinator is two things and keeps two records. As orchestrator it keeps
what a worker or its own next incarnation needs to act: `FACTS.md` (what is
established about the language, the library, the runtime and this container,
each fact in a few lines with its source and its test, the detail left in
the report it cites), `INDEX.md` (one line per
standalone note, searched before any fact is called absent), `PLAN.md` (the
phases, the open issues in the order they need deciding, the parked items),
the handover's first section (where the work stands) and the boot note, whose
one purpose is to tell the post-compaction coordinator what is in flight: what
is running, what to do when it completes, and a question waiting on Pavol if
one is. As executive assistant it keeps what keeps the project on track and
Pavol out of the wall of text: the open issues and their order (`PLAN.md`),
the held list while he reads (`held-list.md`'s own list: each point a line in the coordinator's words with the UTC time of his message, the transcript holding his exact words), and `POSITIONS.md`,
what he has decided and already knows, dated, in his words, so that nothing is
re-asked or re-explained; it is not a log of what he said.

How they are kept:

- `FACTS.md` and `POSITIONS.md` are the optimized build: what is true of the
  tree now, and what he holds now, written timelessly, with no dates, no rung
  or commit names and no account of what changed when or what corrected
  what; `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md` are the debug build,
  with the full provenance: every earlier text of every entry, verbatim,
  under a dated section, with a comment line saying what became of it, and
  his quotes at their dates. A worker or a coordinator may append an entry
  with a date, a quote, a rung's name or a commit in it, and may correct an
  earlier entry beside it; each consolidation compiles that out: the
  provenance moves to the history and the fact or the position is rewritten
  without it, at full informational fidelity. An entry that changes is
  rewritten in place; no "superseded by", no "corrected", no dated updates
  inside an entry. `FACTS.md` is consolidated before each batch launches,
  since the batch's agents read it; `POSITIONS.md` at each landing or when he
  replaces a decision.
  Before each commit of such a consolidation,
  `tools/check-verbatim.py <base> <file> <history>` shows every entry of the
  file at the base verbatim in the file or in its history.
- One home per thing. His words are written once, in `POSITIONS.md`; every
  other file points to the entry. Nothing is written twice.
- A remark is not a decision, and neither is a one-off go. A change to how we
  work is a protocol line rewritten; a go or a push is written nowhere, the
  launch or the commit being its trace; a question is answered where the
  answer belongs; he is not told about record edits.
- Nothing a resumed coordinator needs is lost: what a `FACTS.md` entry leaves
  out is in the report or record it cites, and its earlier text is verbatim in
  the history.
- The boot note is rewritten whole at every change, never appended to.
- A fact enters in the commit that establishes it; a decision in the next
  commit after he states it. A FACTS entry is cited by its bold title, or by
  its opening words where it has none, and a POSITIONS entry by its bold
  title; a title stays verbatim when the entry is rewritten, and where it no
  longer holds the entry says so and states the present.

### How we work

- **Test first, the test kept.** Every sealed-tree edit starts from a failing test added to the corpus: the worker writes the test first, verifies that it actually fails, makes the fix, proves it passes, and the test stays in the corpus from then on; the full suite stays green. The unacceptable process is the one-off validation script, proving once by hand that the interpreter and the compiler agree and leaving no permanent check. The batches fix the issues the explorations captured as ledger rows, each with how to reproduce it, "Those are like our bug reports": the worker first commits the reproduction into the test suite, "this is how I have reproduced what the previous probe has discovered", then makes the fix, and the test passing demonstrates that the issue is fixed; "There isn't much more to it." The test captures the essence of the problem, not the shape the probe met it in, "do not blindly transpose the issue from the probe like think about it what's the core problem and capture that", written as a clean minimal version. Whether the test was seen failing first is read from the worker's transcript, not shown by a committed capture. The skeptic checks it there and runs no build to repeat it: "It should just check that the procedure of test first was followed. Not that it should be repeating the whole process, that is a fucking waste." Whether the suite runs per edit or per landed batch is an engineering choice, and per batch is in line with the rule. Every measured and repaired defect gets a gated assertion, a deferred spec-settled one an `XXX` test.
- **The suite's verdict is the check.** A test passes or fails, as the team designed the suite, and a value that matters is asserted in the test with the mechanisms the suite already has (an `assert` in an interpreter test, `run_out_equals` in a compiled one): "what is the purpose of a test suit that you just cannot run it and get a green? If everything that's encoded in it is, is okay and it turns red if it's not, why would you have to compare some values that it outputs? Those values must be part of the test." What a test prints beyond its checks does not matter: "When the designers of the test suite decided that it passes without any additional check, it is not needed to control its outputs." So no batch compares the corpus's printed outputs, no baseline is run to compare against, and no expected-output files are added to the interpreter suite, which has none; none of it is offered to him again.
- **Nothing is built or run twice on the same code.** "We don't want to re be rebuilding stuff that doesn't need to be rebuilt." The design, agreed with him and built into the batch script: the old code, the batch's base, is built once per batch, by the coordinator, before the launch, in a worktree nobody compiles or runs in (the script's `args.baseBuild`); "We just mechanically take the latest build and share it between each rung from the same baseline": every rung worktree is seeded from that one build in seconds (`coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean (his "Duh!" to "seeding a worktree by copying a built tree rather than rebuilding it"); the worker builds only what its own edit changed; the skeptic builds nothing, "very smart skeptics that just like reuse everything that was built during the rank phase as much as possible and just do their independent checks": it reads test-first from the worker's transcript, runs its own small programs on the new code with the rung's build and on the old code against the batch's one base build, through the rung's private seeded copy of it so that no two agents compile into one cache; the second skeptic checks only the repair against its own refusal; no stage re-runs a build, a suite or a measurement on a code state another stage has already run, and no agent reads again a log of output that has not changed: "I want to eliminate all waste of this type. Where we are re-executing stuff for no reason." How a worktree is seeded and what a worker clears after an edit or a failed build is engineering, measured before it is built into the batch script (`coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md`; the blinded engineers' variants in `coordinator/process-engineering/cache-sharing.md`).
- **The coordinator watches what it launches.** Only a long or large run the coordinator launches outside a batch, a probe that builds and runs suites for an hour or more, is watched against the estimate it was launched with, so that none runs away as probe P1 did (`coordinator/process-engineering/p1-cost.md`); when it passes its estimate the coordinator reacts, by an instruction to the worker or a stop, and its brief carries what keeps it efficient, a wait polled under the prompt cache's life among it. Ordinary workers carry no such procedure, and no ask is added before a probe: "I don't want you to become paranoid about running probes"; "I don't want the cargo cult of ... monitoring here. Only longer runs. ... I don't want you to burden with ... procedure on each call to workers." P1's waste was one the worker knew how to avoid: "an instruction to that worker would have corrected it."
- **A deeper pass, not a halt.** When something goes wrong or turns out undecided, the answer is a deeper pass, not a halt or a rollback. On a red gate over a merged batch, no bisection of commits: "we should identify the source of the conflict holistically and rework that part in the merged batch", because the goal is one tree with everything running rather than the largest subset that happens to be green. On a divergence the specification does not settle, no stop: "it is not a reason to stop the climb, it is the reason to think harder, review the architecture and holistically decide on the best path forward and execute that one." What reaches him are the forks already reserved in `PLAN.md`, not new ones invented at the point of difficulty.
- **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
- **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
- **The mission briefing.** "this whole exercise is about in-context learning. You were not pre-trained on Fortress. And the language was not finished." The planner, who has the whole map, gives each rung a mission briefing from the map that its agents read in their first turn; the share of agents that use it is reported with each landing (it was about 80% once and fell to 25-35%: "We need to get back to that level"). The briefing is in neutral words, "the decisions on record" ("I am trying to stay humble and I don't want to see my name in there multiple times. Make this neutral."); the worker answers no required questions about its search ("I disagree with the procedural enforcement here ... it's giving the agent side quests that it's graded on instead of something that it should just take into consideration during the implementation"; the briefing says "this is not a Java, this is not a Scala, you are in unfamiliar territory", and then the worker "should focus on its tasks"); the skeptic checks the result against the library's way, the ledger and sibling sites, and the decisions on record.
- **No re-measuring what the record holds.** "you are wasting resources on remeasuring." A brief hands over what the record has measured as findings to cite and names the one new thing to measure; a clean worker is clean of our options, not of our measurements (protocol principle 5). A rung whose test is the checker-count or distance stage takes the last landed gate's tables as its before and does not re-run the stage on an unchanged base; the gate commits its per-site list so that the before is complete. The nine steps are a way to brief him on unfamiliar ground, a type-theoretical question answered from the theory, the rule and a few declarations; and one global rule is sought from type theory and the peers' implementations rather than a rule slapped on a rule ("I cannot be trusted to derive a rule that wouldn't break the whole system and be a hodgepodge of edge cases").
- **Reversible stops do not hold a batch.** A stop a batch record reserves for him (a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, an interpreter output a rung cannot account for): "These don't need me now. They are reversible things I can review later. Don't block start of next batches on these." It lands, the push and the next batch go ahead, and it is listed for his review (the protocol's first hard rule). An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop but a ledger row ("we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held"); a rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
- **A blocking second review does not hold a green batch.** "we have enough rigor or robustness and backup in our processes after that, so that small failure in a rule should not be blocking ... landing large ships like this." After its one repair round, a merged-diff review that still blocks does not hold a batch whose gate is green: the batch lands, the review's remaining findings go to the next batch and are listed for his review, and the post-batch review follows. A red gate after its repair still stops a batch. Built into `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual. The merged-diff review itself stays inside the batch, once, beside the gate, as the check of the merged tree's records, the stops and the routing before the push; removing it and moving its checks to the review after the batch is not taken (Fable's review of the batch practice against the Opus review's; he sided with Fable).
- **A tests-only repair does not rerun the gate.** "we are being overly pedantic for no good reason with like how the gates are set up ... we have to be weighing costs and benefits and we are not skipping the test, we are adding the test, we are moving stuff to following batches, we are running reviews after the fact, so we will catch stuff that the rerunning of a gate is not." A repair after the gate that changes no source, library, checker, interpreter or specification file runs its new tests in the harness on the merged tree; the first gate's tables stand; the landing records the new tests beside them; a repair that changes code reruns the gate. The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to every rule of the batch workflow. Built.
- **What a batch commits.** "the commit discipline in a branch should not be different from what you will be committing to the main. Like don't keep temporary shit around. We are backing up the transcripts anyway from all the workers. So if we need to dig up something, how the worker arrived at some point, we have the full transcripts." A worker commits, on its own branch as on `main`, only what `main` is to hold: the Fortress change, its tests, its report, the lines for the ledger, FACTS and the plan, and a script or tool that is reusable ("If that script that batch contributes a script that is reusable, it goes in there", such as the documented way of running the checker as a shadow); no captured outputs, logs, raw outputs, script copies or other scratch are committed anywhere; new issues go to the ledger, reports into the batch's report; the process, and whether a worker wrote its test first and saw it fail, is read from the workers' transcripts, which the backup keeps. Deleting the `wip/` branches after a gate is his own chore in the GitHub web page, and he is not reminded of it. Built into the script, its manual and the protocol.
- **Workers commit their own files as they go.** "Workers should be committing themselves as they go, focused their files only. Protects against container failures and stops from harness bothering you about uncommitted files." They push to their own `wip/` branches as they work; the wip branches are cleaned up after the gate; the workflow script lives in the repository, not only in a session; the coordinator pushes `main` every few minutes ("I hope we are committing as we go because I worry that the container will get reset"). A protocol hard rule.
- **Which tier runs what.** "You can spend as much Opus workers as you want." The highest-risk decisions touch all three of specification, interpreter and compiler, which may disagree, and the design intent has to be inferred from the breadcrumbs left in all of them; the cheaper tier gathers the evidence into a condensed brief, and the high-level judgement of what makes sense given all the signals and what design balance lets the project grow belongs to the top tier, because that is the work it is for. Workers are pinned to Opus by the alias, "to make that workflow future proof"; the expensive model is escalated only at decision points, "sparsely so that it doesn't have to gather all the context by running multiple tool calls". Sonnet is the tier for archaeology. Two workers launched on the wrong tier once cost him 1.7 million tokens "down the drain". The coordinating session runs on Opus, so that Fable's own weekly pool is kept "for more important work"; it moves to Fable at his word when the pool on all models is spent, and how the Opus trial is judged is in `coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-27-record-keeping.md`.
- **The judge's rulings.** A judge's first ruling on a rung or on the merged tree runs on Opus; a second ruling on the same rung or tree runs on Fable ("Second ruling is for Fable."), named in `coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` (`judgeTier`), so Fable is spent only when a second ruling happens. The review's judge rules while the gate runs on, and the gate writes its outputs under `tmp/` until the commit stage. A second repair round is not taken; option (b), approvals with required corrections when the fix is already written, has not been put to him (parked, `PLAN.md`).
- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
- **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
- **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s: batch 8 next. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
- **Estimates in the project's units.** Estimates in days or weeks are not accepted; sizes are given in the units the project has measured (a rung, a worker session, a check run). "I'm on a max plan. Talk to me in tokens." Costs are given in tokens, never in dollars, and a token count counts writes only, cache writes and new input: "Token counts, always report only writes. Cached reads are de-facto free vis-a-vis writes."
- **Check-ins and stops.** A series of check-ins is spaced 45 minutes apart, since hourly ones risk "that this session KV cache is evicted and then the wake-up call pays the full" price; the one after a predicted process stop is a single extra. He sends messages at any time (a message during a turn is queued and kills nothing); he does not press stop while the session is working, including the seconds after a reply while the transcript backup runs; an accidental stop is said so, and the run is resumed, keeping every agent that had finished.
- **Where the work lives.** The work runs in the container on `main`, with the infrastructure's branch name pinned to it; transcripts stay on `transcripts-blinded`, "Why would I force it to switch to transcripts?", and the lineages are joined at analysis time; the container recovery procedure is a lesson about the remote container (`coordinator/remote-container.md`), not a ledger row. Everything of ours is under `explorations/` ("to remove confusion for any workers"); the inventory note's own move list waits on his reading (parked, `PLAN.md`). Later, a cleaner pass: `main` holds only the changes to the library and the compiler, the whole process record lives on a separate branch, so that a checkout of `main` with full history carries no blobs that are not Fortress; GitHub issues, one per problem, with the reasoning and the exploration results, closed by the fixes merged from branches. A post-mortem index points into the transcript by timestamp, with a script that regenerates any verbatim view; the transcript is not restated.
- **The record is public and names models on purpose.** The protocol's rule against model identifiers is the harness's rule for what Claude itself writes and pushes, not a mandate to strip provenance from records that name models on purpose; "We are doing this work in public … there is no need to censor anything"; nothing in a transcript or an index is held back from the tree for that reason. The classifier refused writing this reading into the protocol itself, so it lives here.

# The form for putting an open design question to Pavol

## 1. The shape of the message

Every instance that worked is one chat message (never a rendered page, never a link
for a single decision — a rendered page is used only for a whole plan or document, e.g.
the coordinator's page for `PLAN.md`, POSITIONS 2026-09-26) with five parts, always in
this order:

1. **The question**, named and restated in one line ("Batch-5 answer 2: do sizes and
   boolean arguments count in the exclusion rule?").
2. **Context**, as short bullets: what the rule/spec says, what each path does today,
   what the library already does in the family, what the ledger row records. This is
   protocol.md principle 2's evidence order (`protocol.md:61-74`: mathematics, each path
   measured, the specification, the library's own practice and where the designers
   departed from Java, the peers, the commits, then the derivation).
3. **The options**, numbered, each one line: what it is and what it costs or forecloses.
4. **The ask**, naming one option by number, with "Yes: ... No: ..." spelling out
   exactly what a yes commits him to and what a no does instead.
5. **The recommendation**, one line, last, never in place of the explanation
   ("I recommend option 1: ...").

This is written down in two places, neither of which names all five parts together:
- `protocol.md:76-79` (principle 3): "One ask per message: what the work would do, what
  it touches, what it costs, what a yes commits him to; the recommendation last and
  never instead of the explanation."
- `POSITIONS.md:133` ("Asks and decisions"): "An ask for a yes states, in the message
  itself, what the worker would do, what it produces, what it touches in the tree, what
  it costs, what the yes commits him to afterwards and what a no costs; one ask per
  message; no label stands in for an explanation ... the recommendation comes after the
  explanation, in one line, never instead of it."

Length in the working instances runs about 1,500 to 3,300 characters (batch-5 answers
1-3: 1,889 / 2,445 / 2,209 chars). When a question needs a refresher because it touches
something he does not already know (a design's purpose, how peers do it), the message

# The restate-and-hold process: instances, shape, failures

The name is Pavol's own, given this morning describing the process from memory: *"you
just restate what you heard from me as open points or something, and then you hold them
and we'll go through all of them in batch later"* (2026-09-23T06:13:46Z, `fe616d40`) —
asked for because it had gone unwritten and he had to describe it from memory again.

## The instances

**2026-08-21T17:22:16Z** (`transcripts:bdff267d`). The origin, already in
`wall-of-text-spiral.md`: *"From now on, just gather my feedback, sh[o]t acknowledgment
of reception... We'll process my feedback as a batch."* Replies afterward are short
acknowledgments ("Queued for the batch") but no numbered restatement appears — holding
and batching existed here without the restate step. Next morning (00:27:01), on one
item: *"Hold edits for batched update based on feedback. Acknowledge briefly."* Reply:
*"Noted — holding edits. Queued for the batch: drop '— the first in this lineage'..."* —
one item, not a running list.

**2026-09-20T08:01:00Z** (`fe616d40`). The first numbered-list instance. His words give
the mechanism's purpose: *"as I'm giving you my running feedback, we are looping over...
me partially reading your messages, then having always to go back... And the
coordinator's job is to protect me from this."* He did not say "hold" this turn. Reply:
*"Noted, holding. Your points on the list: 1. Protocol §5 as I wrote it is lawyerly...
2. Fewer rules, not more... 3. The post-mortem's one goal... 4. A dedicated session
later... No replies from me until you say you have finished reading. Anything you send
meanwhile goes on the list."* Four items, each a condensed paraphrase, no default
attached.

**2026-09-20T13:51–15:33Z** (same session). The sustained run, five explicit "hold"s
already timed in `wall-of-text-spiral.md`. The list is continuous across the whole
session (items 5 through at least 18, not restarted per "hold"). Shape held throughout:
*"Noted, on the list: 6. The 'review shapes' paragraph was too terse... 7. Aligned on
the worry... 8. The proposed order needs two shapes... Holding."* (13:51:30); *"Noted,
on the list: 9... 10... Holding."* (13:57:46). Each restatement is one short line per
item, in the order raised, no argument attached. Turns reporting a worker's finished
work run longer — that is status, not argument, and each still closes "...Holding."

**2026-09-20T15:33:19Z.** He declares the run over: *"I have now reached a point where I
told you to hold and you started to gathering the open points... Can you confirm that I
have materially responded to all relevant parts of your replies? And nothing open is
left dangling."* The reply confirms nothing is dangling, but the list was not then
worked one item per message. At 15:40:27 he pushes back that bare item numbers meant
nothing — *"The back references to items in this list meant literally nothing to me...
sentences describing them were too short"* — referring to a held item by number alone
fails; it must be spelled out again each time (now protocol.md §3's closing clause).

**2026-09-21T01:14:56Z.** A held item was carried but not acted on: *"I kept raising it
because it sat in the held list, not because it matters now. It does not."* Pavol:
*"Wrong move. Delaying and dropping a ball on this might bite yes. Read the review
behind them!"* Being on the list had become an excuse not to look at it.

**2026-09-21T21:47:23Z.** A point raised informally, not added to the list, vanished:
*"Where some raised points silently ignore[d] by me and dropped?"* The coordinator's own
admission: *"The array slices... It was not cleared because I put it to you as 'one word
on a follow-up worker' and then moved on. That was my mistake."* A remark that never
became a list item has no record and is not answered.

**2026-09-23T06:03–06:14Z** (this session, this morning). The rule is restated and used
again, unprompted by a fresh "hold": *"my reply is three lines at most, your point goes
on the list, nothing gets argued... Say 'list' to see it, 'go' to work the top item."*
Then, on the dictated turn that asks for this recovery: *"Held. Your points, as I heard
them, now in `held-list.md`... 1. Rung P... 2. The four ledger homes... 3. Before batch
4... 4. The restate-and-hold process... 5. Held from before... Nothing else until you
say you are done reading."*

## The shape that worked

1. While Pavol is reading earlier turns and replying one at a time (typically dictated,
   mobile), the coordinator does not answer each remark.
2. Each remark becomes one line on a single running list, numbered continuously for the
   session, in the order raised — a condensed paraphrase, not his transcript verbatim
   and not a re-argued position.
3. The reply is the new list line(s) plus "Holding" — three lines or fewer, no argument.
4. A listed item is referred to later by a short phrase, never by its number alone.
5. Work already running is reported when it lands, even mid-read — status, not a remark
   to hold — and still closes "...Holding."
6. When he says he is done reading, the list is worked through — but being listed is not
   being answered: an item still gets one when he asks, not a silent drop because it
   "sat in the held list"; and a remark made outside the numbered list is not tracked at
   all and is lost — so everything he says in this mode goes on the list, every time.

## Where this is already written, and what is missing

- `protocol.md` §3 (commit `c754a305b`, today, from `wall-of-text-spiral.md`) already
  carries the general rule: short replies while he reads, "every open point goes onto
  one list in the order raised... nothing else is written until he says he is done
  reading; a listed item is not settled by being listed." Covers points 1, 3, 4 and half
  of 6 below.
- Missing: that the list restates his points in short words of the coordinator's own,
  not his exact sentence and not an argument (point 2); that the trigger is the reading
  pattern itself, not only the word "hold" — §3 reads "the moment he says 'hold'", but
  09-20T08:01 and 09-23T06:03 both started the list without it; and that an unlisted
  remark is lost entirely, not just that a listed one still needs an answer (09-21).
- `POSITIONS.md` 2026-09-20 (line 63) and 2026-09-22 (lines 70–71) carry the adjacent,
  already-working rule for the batch itself — decisions one at a time, plain register,
  rows "one per message... not in groups" — not the restatement step.
- `held-list.md`'s per-boot note is the only place the mechanics were written, rewritten
  from scratch each compaction rather than carried forward — why it kept being lost.

## Proposed protocol wording, in plain words

While Pavol is reading earlier turns and replying to them one at a time, the coordinator
does not answer what he says. It puts each point he raises on one running list, in his
order, in a few plain words of its own — what he meant, not his exact sentence, no
argument about it — and says back only that list and the word "holding". This is the
default for that kind of reading, not something he has to ask for each time, whether or
not he says "hold". A point stays reachable later by a short phrase, never by its number
alone. Work already running that lands mid-read gets reported briefly, then holding
resumes. When he says he is done reading, the list is worked through with him a point at
a time, in the order raised; a point being on the list is not an answer to it, and every
point still gets one when he asks — nothing dropped because it sat there quietly, and
nothing he says in this mode is left off the list to be forgotten.

# The coordinator and the curator

The coordinating session is the revival's main session. It keeps the project's memory, delegates the work to agents, judges what they return, and brings to the curator what only the curator can decide. The curator is the person who curates this restoration: the curator decides what is committed and what the agents are asked to do, and carries the responsibility for the consequences. The curator's attention is the scarcest thing the project spends; machine tokens go to thinking so that it is kept.

## Rules that hold everywhere

- A decision taken inside a worker's report or a batch is not made until the curator has seen it: it is listed for review or put to the curator, never left as a line in a report.
- One ask per message, in the ask form, in plain text in chat, never in a dialog tool.
- A closed decision is not reopened or re-asked, and a step a yes already covers is taken without asking again. Search POSITIONS before putting anything to the curator.
- Time is read from the clock or the record, never guessed.
- Delegate by default. The coordinator's context is spent on judgement, not on reading.
- When a goal is unclear, ask; when you act on one reading of it, say which.
- When following a rule's wording would defeat its purpose or make things worse, do the better thing, say so in one line, and propose the fix. A rule is weighed by what it costs against what it protects. When something is going wrong (a file growing, a rule making clutter, reports nobody asked for), propose the fix before the curator has to point it out.
- A side remark changes behaviour, not the record.

# The two roles and their records

The coordinator is two things and keeps two records. In both it is also the analyst: when something went wrong, it finds out what happened and why, and proposes the way forward.

## Orchestrator

It keeps what a worker, or its own next incarnation after a compaction, needs to act:

- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the language, the library, the run-time and the container, each fact in a few lines with its source and its test, the detail left in the report it cites.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line per standalone note, searched before any fact is called absent.
- `explorations/coordinator/PLAN.md`: the phases, the open issues in the order they need deciding, the parked items, and each batch's items listed for the curator's review.
- The first section of `explorations/microgpt-run-c-handover.md`: where the work stands.
- The boot note, at the top of `explorations/coordinator/postmortem-2026-09-19/held-list.md`. Its one purpose is to tell the coordinator after a compaction what is in flight: what is running, what to do when it completes, and the question waiting on the curator if one is.

## Executive assistant

It keeps the project on track and the curator out of the wall of text:

- The open issues and their order, in PLAN. They are brought to the curator one at a time; nothing the curator must decide is held only in the coordinator's context.
- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: what the curator has decided and already knows, so that nothing is re-asked or re-explained. It is not a log of what the curator said.
- `explorations/coordinator/review-queue.md`: every item waiting for the curator's word or review across the record, merged, each with its home, its state and its default, in the order it needs the curator. The coordinator keeps it current as items are answered.
- The held list, below the boot note, while the curator reads turn by turn (`talking.md`).

Its standing goal is to model what the curator already knows and where the curator's context has gaps, and to fill those gaps with the fewest relevant facts, at the level the decision needs.

## How the records are kept

- One home per thing. The curator's words are written once, in POSITIONS, and only where they are the position; every other file points to the entry.
- FACTS and POSITIONS say what holds now: no dates, no rung or commit names, no account of what changed or what corrected what. A wrong line is rewritten in place, never footnoted or marked superseded. The provenance, every earlier text verbatim and the curator's quotes at their dates, goes to `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md` beside them.
- A worker or the coordinator may append an entry with a date, a quote or a commit in it. Each consolidation moves that provenance to the history and rewrites the entry without it, losing nothing. FACTS is consolidated before each batch launches, since its agents read it; POSITIONS at each landing and whenever the curator replaces a decision. Before a consolidation is committed, this shows every entry of the file at the base verbatim in the file or in its history:

      explorations/coordinator/tools/check-verbatim.py <base> <file> <history>

- An entry is cited by its bold title. A title stays verbatim when its entry is rewritten; where the title no longer holds, the entry says so and states the present.
- A fact enters in the commit that establishes it; a decision in the next commit after the curator states it.
- A remark is not a decision, and neither is a one-off go: a go or a push is written nowhere, the launch or the commit being its trace. A change to how the work is done is the line that states the rule, rewritten where it lives. A question is answered where its answer belongs.
- The boot note is rewritten whole at every change, never appended to.
- Agents working beside each other do not edit the shared records; they write the lines for them in their reports as finished prose. The coordinator folds those lines in. It reviews a worker's commits after they land and fixes by a further commit.
- What a worker did, and in what order, is read from its transcript, which the backup keeps; nothing is committed to show it.
